title: Layered Architecture
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of layered architecture in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply layered architecture to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: Layered Architecture is lesson 194 in Design Patterns and Application Architecture. A layered design separates UI or API delivery, use cases, domain rules, and infrastructure details. Dependencies should point toward stable rules, and the project should avoid layers that do not protect a real boundary.
content.why_it_matters: Patterns are options, not goals. Start from the problem and choose the smallest design that keeps change local. This lesson focuses on layered architecture and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A layered design separates UI or API delivery, use cases, domain rules, and infrastructure details. Dependencies should point toward stable rules, and the project should avoid layers that do not protect a real boundary.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for layered architecture. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates layered architecture. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates layered architecture rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for layered architecture before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
